newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Sihanouk signs pardon for Khmer Rouge leader.
newsitem.headline: Sihanouk signs pardon for Khmer Rouge leader.

text.p: Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk pardoned dissident Khmer Rouge leader Ieng Sary on Saturday for his role in the notorious "killing fields" era of the late 1970s, one of the country's two co-premiers said.
Ieng Sary was foreign minister to dictator Pol Pot during the murderous Khmer Rouge regime of 1975-79 when more than one million people died.
"His majesty the king signed the amnesty...with the support of two thirds of (the members of) parliament," Second Prime Minister Hun Sen told Reuters.
Cambodia's two premiers had asked for the pardon in the interests of national reconciliation.
Ieng Sary split from the Khmer Rouge last month with several thousand followers and later struck a ceasefire deal with the government.
But the hardline Khmer Rouge faction loyal to Pol Pot has condemned the breakaway group and remains at war.
The Khmer Rouge signed a United Nations brokered peace accord in 1991 but later reneged on the pact and have been fighting the coalition government that emerged from general elections in 1991.
Hun Sen said it had been easy to collect the signatures from MPs in the 120-member national assembly as he and First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh were leaders of the two main parties.

Hun Sen is the deputy leader of the Cambodian People's Party, which holds 51 seats, while the prince is president of the royalist FUNCINPEC party with 58 seats. Two smaller parties, also in the government, hold the remaining seats.
Information Ministry Secretary of State Khieu Kanharith confirmed Sihanouk had signed an amnesty.

Sihanouk had earlier said however that, despite any pardon, he would still support the convening and outcome of any international tribunal called to try the leaders of the Khmer Rouge regime, including Pol Pot and Ieng Sary.
Ieng Sary, who was sentenced to death in absentia for his role in the genocide, denied on Monday that he was involved in any killings.
Hun Sen said the amnesty would help finish off the Maoist Khmer Rouge.
"I consider that this is a golden opportunity for the Cambodian people to end the war and for national reconciliation," he said.

A working committee of senior military officials of the government and the breakaway guerrilla faction in northwest Cambodia would meet in the next few days to discuss how to join forces and open up their territory.
Hardliners in the northern Khmer Rouge base of Anlong Veng would be "shaking wildly because of this national reconciliation,' Hun Sen added.
